items.title: Arbitrary-level cyclotomic Hecke, Murphy cell and multipartition Schur modules
items.statement:
Let R be a commutative ring, n≥0, ℓ≥1, and z,U_1,...,U_ℓ units of R. Define H_n by commuting invertible X_1,...,X_n, finite generators T_i satisfying (T_i−z)(T_i+1)=0, the type-A braid/distant relations, T_iX_iT_i=zX_(i+1), distant mixed commutation, and ∏_a(X_1−U_a)=0. For n=0 set H_0=R. The grading variable v is not z. An ℓ-multipartition λ of n is an ordered tuple of partitions; dominance compares every cumulative component/row sum. Fill tλ in component,row,column order. Put a_k=Σ_(b<k)|λ^(b)|, uλ=∏_k∏_(j≤a_k)(X_j−U_k), xλ=Σ_(w∈Sλ)T_w, mλ=xλuλ, Mλ=mλH_n. The row subgroup Sλ stabilizes the rows of tλ. The presentation involution * fixes all X_j,T_i and reverses products. For standard s,t of shapeλ put m_st=T_d(s)*mλT_d(t), where tλd(s)=s. Denote by H^{>λ} the span of higher Murphy shapes once their basis/cell law is established by [[thm-arbitrary-level-cyclotomic-hecke-murphy-basis-is-cellular]], and Sλ the right cell/Specht module with basis m_t and action from that cell law. Its cellular form defines Dλ=Sλ/radSλ; Dλ may vanish.

Types are EXACTLY all ℓ-multipartitions of n, including empty components, not all multicompositions. A semistandard tableau S has labels (row,component) ordered by component then row, weak rows, strict columns, and a label of component a can occur only in physical component b≤a; its type counts each label with the multiplicity of that multipartition row. For a standard s, µ(s) replaces each entry by its row/component in tµ. Set m_(S,t)=Σ_(s:µ(s)=S)m_st and m_(S,T)=Σ_(s,t:µ(s)=S,ν(t)=T)m_st. Define M=⊕_(λ multipartition of n)Mλ and C_n=End_(H_n)(M), with ordinary composition. For S,T of shapeλ and typesµ,ν, the map φ_ST, once justified by [[lem-cyclotomic-semistandard-sums-give-schur-endomorphism-basis]], sends mαh to δ_(α,ν)m_(S,T)h. Its right cell module ∆λ has basis v_T for semistandard T of multipartition types, contravariant cell form and quotient Lλ. Let Tλ be the unique tableau of shape/typeλ, and let eλ be the identity projection onto Mλ. Put ω=(∅,...,∅,(1^n)) and e=eω; mω=1, so Mω=H_n. In particular H_n is an actual direct summand of M. Weight projections for Jantzen theory are eν with ν multipartition. Define K_(λ,ν)=#SStdν(λ). All asserted module/form/map laws are discharged by the linked local theorem/lemma suppliers; the definition itself does not claim their proofs or the primitive residue-content classification.

items.title: Laurent binomial valuation at one over any field
items.statement: For nonzero A,B in F and integers u,v, the valuation of A t^u-B t^v is zero if A!=B. If A=B and N=u-v!=0, it is 1 in characteristic zero, and p^{v_p(|N|)} in characteristic p>0. If A=B and N=0 the polynomial is zero and does not have finite valuation.
items.strategy:
**Statement.** For nonzero A,B in F and integers u,v, the valuation of A t^u-B t^v is zero if A!=B. If A=B and N=u-v!=0, it is 1 in characteristic zero, and p^{v_p(|N|)} in characteristic p>0. If A=B and N=0 the polynomial is zero and does not have finite valuation.

**Proof.** Multiplication by B t^v is a unit, so reduce to (A/B)t^N-1. If A/B!=1 its value at t=1 is nonzero. When A=B replace negative N by -N by multiplying by the unit -t^N. If char F=0, t^N-1=(t-1)(1+t+...+t^{N-1}), and the second factor evaluates to N!=0. In characteristic p, write N=p^r m with p not dividing m. Frobenius gives t^N-1=(t^m-1)^{p^r}; the same geometric-series factor for t^m-1 evaluates to the nonzero element m. The valuation is p^r. The zero case is immediate.

In the intended J expression, foot residues are Q_a q_H^{j-i} t^{na+j-i}. This leaf computes their difference exactly when it is nonzero and prevents replacing valuations by an equality-of-residues indicator in positive characteristic.

items.title: Ultra-tight multisets admit integer column potentials
items.statement: Let $r\ge1$ and $L_r=\mathbb Z^r/\mathbb Z(1,\ldots,1)$. For a finite multiset $X$ in $L_r$, call $X$ tight if $(x_k-x_l)-(y_k-y_l)\le2$ for all occurrences $x,y$ and indices $k,l$. A zero exchange replaces $x,y$ by $x-e_k+e_l,y+e_k-e_l$ when that difference equals2; it is symmetric. Call $X$ ultra-tight if every finite zero-exchange sequence ends in a tight multiset. Then $X$ is ultra-tight iff some $s\in\mathbb Z^r$ satisfies $x_k-x_l\le s_k-s_l+1$ for every $x\in X,k,l$. This includes the empty multiset and $r=1$.
items.strategy:
For the empty multiset take s=0. For nonempty X the complete finite induction follows.

Work in L_r=Z^r/Z(1,…,1). A finite multiset X is tight if

(x_k−x_l)−(y_k−y_l)≤2 for every x,y∈X and every k,l.

A zero exchange replaces x,y by x−e_k+e_l and y+e_k−e_l when the displayed difference equals 2. This relation is symmetric; call X ultra-tight if every multiset obtainable by finitely many zero exchanges is tight. These notions do not depend on representatives in Z^r.

**Lemma.** X is ultra-tight iff there are integers s₁,…,s_r such that x_k−x_l≤s_k−s_l+1 for every x∈X and every k,l.

The reverse implication has a short direct proof. After replacing x by x−s, every row has maximum minus minimum at most one. A zero exchange must have x_k−x_l=1 and y_k−y_l=−1, so it merely swaps the high and low values in these two coordinates of each row. The row spread remains at most one. The property is preserved by every zero exchange and implies tightness.

Here is a full proof of the forward implication, adapted from the actual proof of Fayers Proposition 2.2 and its induction step Proposition 2.3 (author PDF pp.11–15). We induct on r. The r=1 case is trivial. Projection forgetting the last coordinate takes an ultra-tight multiset to one in L_(r−1): every zero exchange in the projection lifts using the same pair of coordinate indices and the same labeled multiset occurrences. Hence the induction hypothesis supplies potentials for the first r−1 coordinates. It remains to extend them to coordinate r, preserving all previous bounds.

Write a_kl=s_k−s_l. Suppose bounds |(x_k−x_l)−a_kl|≤1 are known whenever k,l≤r−1 or k,l≥t+1, with 1≤t≤r−1. We show how to obtain such bounds also for k,l≥t. For t=r−1, tightness says the integer differences x_(r−1)−x_r have range at most two, so choose their integer midpoint for s_(r−1)−s_r; the potentials on the first r−1 coordinates stay fixed.

For t<r−1, if the current potentials already bound x_t−x_r, nothing is needed. Otherwise, after replacing every row x and every potential s by its negative if necessary, choose x∈X with x_t−x_r≥a_tr+2. For t<u<r, the old bounds imply x_t−x_u≤a_tu+1 and x_u−x_r≤a_ur+1. Thus x_t−x_r=a_tr+2, and both inequalities are equalities for every u. Tightness implies, for every y∈X,

a_tr≤y_t−y_r≤a_tr+2.

Form a directed graph on {1,…,r}, with an edge k→l when some y∈X has y_k−y_l=a_kl−1.

If no path leads from t to r, let T be the vertices reachable from t and let R be the complement. Change potentials to s'_k=s_k+1 for k∈T and s'_k=s_k for k∈R. Then a'_tr=a_tr+1, giving the new (t,r) bound. Any other previously controlled difference with a'_kl≥a_kl retains its upper bound. If a'_kl=a_kl−1, then k∈R,l∈T. The reverse pair has no edge T→R, so its old lower bound y_l−y_k≥a_lk−1 improves to ≥a_lk; hence y_k−y_l≤a_kl=a'_kl+1. Apply this to ordered pairs and their reverses. All required bounds hold.

If a path does lead from t to r, choose a shortest path t=k₁→k₂→⋯→k_h=r and labeled occurrences y₁,…,y_(h−1) witnessing its edges. Its vertices are distinct. Write z=y−s for each witness. On the first r−1 coordinates every such z has spread at most one, by the old bounds. Therefore one occurrence cannot witness two edges both ending before r: their low-to-high values would give the shortcut k_m→k_(n+1) for m<n. Nor can it witness an earlier edge and the last edge: a last-edge witness has z_(k_(h−1))=z_r−1; tightness against the chosen x gives z_k−z_r≥−1 for every k<r, while spread at most one on the first r−1 coordinates gives z_k−z_r≤0. An earlier edge witnessed by the same row would thus start at z_r−1, giving a shortcut from its starting vertex directly to r. Hence all edge witnesses are distinct occurrences.

For each k<r, x_k−x_r≥a_kr+1: for k≥t this was proved above, and for k<t use x_k−x_t≥a_kt−1 and x_t−x_r=a_tr+2. Put x^(m)=x−e_(k_(m+1))+e_r for 1≤m<h. At m=h−1 this is x itself. We first note why none of the edge witnesses can be the chosen occurrence x. If y_p=x, choose such a p (at most one, since edge witnesses are distinct). It cannot be the last witness, since its edge to r would have x_(k_(h−1))−x_r=a_(k_(h−1),r)−1, contradicting the preceding lower bound. Run the following downward exchange induction using only witnesses with index >p, all distinct from x and from each other. It yields x_(k_(p+1))−x_r=a_(k_(p+1),r)+1. Combining this with x_(k_p)−x_r≥a_(k_p,r)+1 gives x_(k_p)−x_(k_(p+1))≥a_(k_p,k_(p+1)), incompatible with y_p=x witnessing the value a_(k_p,k_(p+1))−1. Thus no witness equals x. This use of the induction is valid on the shorter tail because it needs only its current distinguished row and the tail witnesses, whose occurrences survive all earlier tail exchanges.

Here is that downward induction in full. We prove that some multiset equivalent to X contains x^(m) and the unchanged witnesses y₁,…,y_m, and that x_(k_m)−x_r=a_(k_m,r)+1. The base uses the original X: tightness between x and y_(h−1) says their (k_(h−1),r) differences, which differ by at least two, differ by exactly two, forcing the claimed equality and giving a permitted zero exchange for the next stage. For the induction step, perform the zero exchange between x^(m+1) and y_(m+1) in coordinates k_(m+1),k_(m+2). It creates x^(m) and leaves all earlier witnesses unchanged because their occurrences are distinct. For m≤h−2 neither k_m nor k_(m+1) is r. The already proved equality at k_(m+1), and the lower bound at k_m, give

x^(m)_(k_m)−x^(m)_(k_(m+1)) ≥ a_(k_m,k_(m+1))+1 = (y_m,_(k_m)−y_m,_(k_(m+1)))+2.

The resulting multiset is tight by ultra-tightness. Therefore equality holds, supplying the next zero exchange and forcing x_(k_m)−x_r=a_(k_m,r)+1. This completes the induction.
At m=1 the conclusion is x_t−x_r=a_tr+1, contradicting x_t−x_r=a_tr+2. Therefore an ultra-tight multiset cannot fall in this second case.

This extends the bounds at each t=r−1,r−2,…,1. The r induction proves the lemma. The proof uses only finite multisets and integer arithmetic.

items.title: Affine type-A presentations and charged cyclotomic quotients
items.statement: Let A be a commutative base ring and z a unit. The nondegenerate AFFINE presentation has commuting units X_r and finite generators T_r with T_r²=(z−1)T_r+z, braid/distant relations, T_rX_rT_r=zX_(r+1) and T_rX_s=X_sT_r for s not r,r+1. The degenerate AFFINE presentation over A has commuting x_r and symmetric-group generators s_r, with s_r x_r=x_(r+1)s_r−1, s_r x_(r+1)=x_r s_r+1 and distant mixed commutation. Auxiliary cyclotomic quotients impose a monic polynomial f of degree ℓ only on the first polynomial generator, with unit constant term in NG. Rank zero is A; degree-zero f=1 at positive rank gives zero. For the charged CYCLIC specialization take A=F a field, z=q_H of finite quantum characteristic e>=2, I=Z/eZ an integer LABEL set, λ_i>=0 and ℓ=Σ_iλ_i (a dominant cyclic type-A weight). If q_H!=1 use NG and c_i=q_H^i; if q_H=1 (charF=e) use DG and c_i=i·1_F. Impose f(z_1)=∏_i(z_1−c_i)^{λ_i} to define H^Λ_d. This charged finite-e branch is the native24 scope; the arbitrary-base affine/monic definitions supply its necessary universal PBW/trace proof inputs. No basis, spectrum, primitive blocks or BK isomorphism is asserted by this pure definition. The grading variable v is independent of q_H.
items.strategy: Explicit generators/relations and the quotient ideal define these algebras. The distinct NG values follow from multiplicative order e, while DG integers are distinct because e=charF; no embedding Z/eZ→F is claimed in NG. The source/KLR grading variable v is independent of q_H.

items.title: DVR cellular Jantzen filtration and exact Gram valuation
items.statement: Let O be a DVR with uniformizer pi and residue field F. Let M be a finite free O-module with an O-valued bilinear pairing b whose scalar extension to Frac(O) is nondegenerate. Set M(s)={x:b(x,M) subset pi^s O} and M_F^s=(M(s)+pi M)/pi M. Then M_F^0=M/pi M, M_F^1=rad(b_F), the filtration terminates, and sum_{s>0}dim_F M_F^s=nu_pi(det G) for any Gram matrix G. If A acts on M with anti-involution * and b(ax,y)=b(x,a* y), all M(s), and hence M_F^s, are submodules. If M_F is a cellular standard module with nonzero cellular form, rad(b_F) is its unique maximal submodule and therefore its module radical.
items.strategy:
**Statement.** Let O be a DVR with uniformizer pi and residue field F. Let M be a finite free O-module with an O-valued bilinear pairing b whose scalar extension to Frac(O) is nondegenerate. Set M(s)={x:b(x,M) subset pi^s O} and M_F^s=(M(s)+pi M)/pi M. Then M_F^0=M/pi M, M_F^1=rad(b_F), the filtration terminates, and sum_{s>0}dim_F M_F^s=nu_pi(det G) for any Gram matrix G. If A acts on M with anti-involution * and b(ax,y)=b(x,a* y), all M(s), and hence M_F^s, are submodules. If M_F is a cellular standard module with nonzero cellular form, rad(b_F) is its unique maximal submodule and therefore its module radical.

**Proof.** View the form as an O-linear map phi:M -> M*=Hom_O(M,O), x -> b(x,-). Its determinant is nonzero, so it has full rank. A direct Smith reduction needs no characteristic restriction: choose a nonzero matrix entry of least valuation, move it to the upper-left corner, and multiply its row by a unit to make it pi^a. Every entry is divisible by pi^a. Row and column subtraction eliminate its column and row, leaving a smaller matrix over O. Iterate. Since all elimination coefficients belong to O and every operation is invertible over O, this gives independent bases of M and M* in which phi sends u_j to pi^{a_j}v_j, with all a_j>=0. Thus

$$M(s)=\bigoplus_j\pi^{\max(0,s-a_j)}O u_j,\qquad \dim_F M_F^s=\#\{j:a_j\ge s\}.$$

Consequently M_F^s=0 for s>max_j a_j and sum_{s>0}dim M_F^s=sum_j a_j=nu_pi(det G). Reduction mod pi shows directly that M(1)/its reduction consists of exactly the vectors orthogonal to every vector of M_F, proving M_F^1=rad(b_F). Contravariance gives b(ax,y)=b(x,a*y) in pi^s O whenever x in M(s), proving stability.

For the last assertion use the defining cellular multiplication, not merely the word cellularity: in the standard module, for every basis label u and label v the corresponding cell element acts as w -> b_F(v,w)u (with left/right conventions transposed if necessary). If a submodule N contains w outside rad(b_F), choose v with b_F(v,w) !=0. Every basis vector u belongs to N by this rank-one action, so N=M_F. Therefore every proper submodule is contained in rad(b_F). The radical itself is proper because the form is nonzero, and the same argument shows the quotient is simple. It is the unique maximal submodule and equals the module radical. This completes the proof, including characteristic 2: the Smith reduction uses different domain and codomain bases, never diagonalization of a symmetric form.

items.title: Universal nondegenerate affine Hecke PBW before the cyclotomic quotient
items.statement: For the affine presentation associated to [[def-arbitrary-level-cyclotomic-hecke-murphy-cell-and-schur-modules]] over the universal Laurent parameter ring R, without imposing the first-variable cyclotomic relation, both families X^aT_w and T_wX^a, a∈Z^n,w∈S_n, are R-bases. Left multiplication by any nonzero Laurent polynomial is injective. Localizing at variable differences embeds this algebra into its rational crossed product; Φ_i=T_i−(z−1)X_(i+1)/(X_(i+1)−X_i) obeys Φ_i f=s_i(f)Φ_i. No cyclotomic basis, BK theorem, trace or primitive-content assertion is used.
items.strategy:
## 1. Affine PBW and the localization used only to prove divisibility

Here is a local PBW proof so that polynomial divisibility does not depend on an unproved affine independence assertion. Bernstein commutation moves every polynomial to the left, and the finite standard-basis relations then give spanning by `X^a T_w`. Set

`c_ij=(z-1)X_j/(X_j-X_i)` and `d_ij=(X_j-zX_i)/(X_j-X_i)`.

In the rational crossed product of the polynomial fraction field with S_n, represent `T_i=c_(i,i+1)+d_(i,i+1)s_i`. These operators satisfy Bernstein commutation and the finite Hecke relations. The quadratic relation uses `c_ij+c_ji=z-1` and `d_ij d_ji=z+(z-1)c_ij-c_ij²`. For three distinct variables the single identity

`c_ij c_jk=c_ik(c_ij+c_jk-(z-1))`

proves the braid relation: coefficients of the longest permutation are both `d_ij d_ik d_jk`; coefficients of the two length2 permutations agree by commutativity; the two length1 coefficients reduce to that displayed identity; the identity coefficient reduces to `(c_ij-c_jk)[c_ij c_jk-c_ik(c_ij+c_jk-(z-1))]=0`. Distant generators involve disjoint variable pairs. These equalities are obtained by substituting their displayed rational functions and clearing the three nonzero differences. Thus this is an actual representation of the universal presentation.

For a reduced word w, the coefficient of its permutation in T_w is a nonzero product of d-functions. All other terms are proper Bruhat subwords. Distinct permutations are independent in the crossed product; if desired this is verified as operators by applying a putative dependence to powers of `f=Σ_j j X_j`: the distinct polynomials w(f) form a Vandermonde matrix over the fraction field. A maximal Bruhat term in a putative PBW dependence therefore has nonzero leading coefficient and cannot cancel. This proves independence and hence affine PBW. The same argument gives right PBW by the involution. In particular left multiplication by a nonzero element of P is injective. All this occurs over the universal characteristic-zero domain; its actual polynomial identities then specialize.

Localize P at the differences `X_i-X_j`, i≠j. Define

`Φ_i=T_i-c_(i,i+1)`.

The Bernstein relation gives `Φ_i f=s_i(f)Φ_i` for every polynomial or localized rational f. Expanding a reduced word T_w as a product of Φ_i+c_i shows that `T_w f` is a sum of terms each containing `v(f)` on the left, where v is the permutation of a subword of that reduced word, multiplied by a coefficient whose only denominators are products of variable differences. Every such v is Bruhat-below w: deletion of adjacent cancelling pairs reduces a subword to a reduced subexpression, or equivalently the standard subword characterization gives this inequality. No denominators `U_a-U_b`, quantum factorials, or Gram determinants are inverted.

items.title: Bounded ordered monomials span cyclotomic type-A Hecke algebras
items.statement: Over any commutative base ring $A$ with invertible nondegenerate parameter, use the defining relations of [[def-type-a-affine-presentations-and-charged-cyclotomic-quotients]], writing $q_H$ for the nondegenerate Hecke parameter. For a monic degree-$\ell>0$ cyclotomic polynomial $f$, with unit constant term in the nondegenerate branch, the quotient by $f(X_1)=0$ is spanned by $X_1^{a_1}\cdots X_d^{a_d}T_w$, and the degenerate quotient by $f(x_1)=0$ is spanned by $x_1^{a_1}\cdots x_d^{a_d}w$, where $0\le a_r<\ell$ and $w\in S_d$. In particular, over a field F each quotient has dimension at most $\ell^d d!$. This applies to $f(t)=\prod_{i\in I}(t-q_H^i)^{\lambda_i}$ and $f(t)=\prod_{i\in I}(t-i)^{\lambda_i}$ in the two finite-quantum-characteristic branches, with $\ell=\sum_i\lambda_i$. No independence or separate relation $f(X_r)=0$ or $f(x_r)=0$ for $r>1$ is asserted. If $\ell=0,d>0$, the relation $1=0$ gives the zero algebra with empty spanning family; for $d=0$ the algebra is $A$ with singleton empty monomial.
items.strategy:
## Elementary straightening input

Only spanning by affine ordered monomials is needed. Move a polynomial past a simple generator using

- NG: T_r p=(s_r p)T_r−(q_H−1)X_{r+1}(p−s_r p)/(X_r−X_{r+1});
- DG: s_r p=(s_r p)s_r−(p−s_r p)/(x_r−x_{r+1}).

Here the first s_r on each right side permutes variables. Both divided differences are polynomials; the NG identity preserves total polynomial degree and the DG correction lowers it by one. The identities follow for a generator variable directly from the mixed relations, and the product case follows by the divided-difference product rule; induction gives every polynomial. Commute distant generators, braid adjacent generators, and reduce quadratic squares to obtain a linear combination of the finite standard words T_w (respectively w). The needed finite Coxeter reduced-word/Hecke straightening supplier is independent of cyclotomic basis or BK. Independence of the affine words is not used.

In NG inverse variables do not present a problem: f(X_1)=0 has nonzero constant term, so X_1^{-1} is a polynomial in X_1. Also X_r=q_H^{1−r}T_{r−1}⋯T_1 X_1 T_1⋯T_{r−1}; inversion expresses X_r^{-1} using X_1^{-1} and T_i^{-1}=q_H^{-1}(T_i−q_H+1). Thus the quotient is generated by positive X's and T's. The positive-polynomial straightening just proved applies.

## NG transported relations and terminating reduction

Put R_1=f(X_1) and R_{r+1}=T_r R_r T_r. Every R_r is zero in the quotient. Ordered straightening gives

R_r=q_H^{r−1}X_r^ℓ+Σ_{a,w} c_{a,w}X_1^{a_1}⋯X_r^{a_r}T_w,

where w∈S_r, Σ_j a_j≤ℓ, and a_r<ℓ. No variable with index above r occurs. Prove this by induction. For a positive integer m, direct summation of the mixed relation gives

T_r X_r^m T_r=q_H X_{r+1}^m−(q_H−1)Σ_{k=1}^{m−1}X_r^k X_{r+1}^{m−k}T_r.

For m=0, T_r²=(q_H−1)T_r+q_H. Hence transporting the displayed leading term produces exactly q_H^r X_{r+1}^ℓ and terms of X_{r+1}-degree below ℓ. For an old remainder monomial, its coefficient has X_r-degree a_r<ℓ. All variables below r commute with T_r, while its T_w lies in the finite H_r and commutes with X_{r+1}. The formula for T_r X_r^{a_r}, followed by finite Hecke straightening of the words T_r T_w T_r and T_w T_r, yields X_{r+1}-degree at most a_r<ℓ. Total degree stays at most ℓ. This proves the induction without assigning f to every X_r.

Order exponent vectors lexicographically as (a_d,a_{d−1},…,a_1), with larger first differing coordinate larger. This is a well-order on N^d and is preserved by addition. If a_r≥ℓ, multiply the zero relation R_r on the left by X^{a−ℓ e_r} and on the right by T_w. Its leading term is q_H^{r−1}X^a T_w. All other terms have the same coordinates above r and a strictly smaller r coordinate, regardless of increases below r. Finite Hecke straightening changes no dot exponents. Since q_H^{r−1} is invertible, solve for X^a T_w in terms of smaller exponent vectors. Well-founded induction terminates and expresses it using only vectors with every coordinate below ℓ. This proves actual bounded ordered spanning.

## DG transported relations and terminating reduction

Put R_1=f(x_1), R_{r+1}=s_r R_r s_r. Straightening and induction show

R_r=x_r^ℓ+Σ_{a,w}c_{a,w}x^a w,

where w∈S_r, all occurring variables have index at most r, and Σ_j a_j<ℓ. Indeed conjugation transports the leading x_r^ℓ to x_{r+1}^ℓ plus correction terms of degree ℓ−1, because

s_r x_r^m s_r=x_{r+1}^m−Σ_{k=0}^{m−1}x_r^k x_{r+1}^{m−1−k}s_r.

Every old remainder remains of degree below ℓ under straightening. If a_r≥ℓ, multiply R_r by x^{a−ℓ e_r} and w; solve for x^a w. Each remainder has total degree strictly below Σ a_j. Induction on total degree proves bounded ordered spanning. In particular this does not falsely claim f(x_r)=0: for level one f(t)=t, x_1=0 implies x_2=s_1, consistently with the formula.

items.title: Cellular nonzero-form heads classify simples and control block linkage
items.statement: For a finite-dimensional cellular algebra over a field F, every nonzero cell-form quotient Dλ is an absolutely simple head, all simples occur exactly once this way, and [Cλ:Dµ]≠0 implies λ≥µ, with [Cµ:Dµ]=1 when Dµ≠0. Nonzero quotient means nonzero form, not necessarily nondegenerate form on Cλ. Every nonzero cell module, including zero-form labels, has all factors in one block. Two cell modules share a block exactly when they are linked by a finite chain of cell modules whose neighboring terms share a simple factor. For one primitive idempotent eµ per simple, dim eµAeν=Σλ[Cλ:Dµ][Cλ:Dν].
items.strategy:
## 1. Cell forms and all simple labels

Let A be a finite-dimensional cellular F-algebra with basis `c_st^λ`, higher ideals `A^{>λ}`, and right cell modules Cλ. Multiplication and its involution show that the coefficient of `c_uv^λ` in `c_us^λ c_tv^λ` modulo higher shapes is a scalar `Gλ(s,t)` independent of u,v. Indeed the right cell axiom first leaves the first index u unchanged, and the left axiom then leaves the last index v unchanged; comparing the two expansions leaves only that common index pair. The involution gives `Gλ(s,t)=Gλ(t,s)`. Associativity of three factors yields `<x a,y>=<x,y a*>`. Consequently the radical Rλ of this finite Gram matrix is a submodule, and the rank-one action is `x c_uv^λ=<x,c_u> c_v`.

If the form is nonzero, any vector outside Rλ has nonzero pairing with some u; after scaling and using the rank-one operators it generates every basis vector of Cλ. Therefore every proper submodule is contained in Rλ, and `Dλ=Cλ/Rλ` is a nonzero simple head with unique maximal submodule Rλ. Extending the field preserves the Gram rank and these rank-one operators, so Dλ is absolutely simple. The correct criterion is **nonzero form**, not nondegenerate form on Cλ. Degenerate but nonzero forms are allowed. No questionable “nonzero iff nondegenerate” clause from another contract is consumed.

To exhaust the simples, let D be any simple A-module. Pick a cell ideal `Iλ=A^{≥λ}` that acts nontrivially on D and is maximal in the finite cell order among such ideals. All strictly higher ideals then annihilate D. Thus the cell layer `Jλ=Iλ/A^{>λ}` acts nontrivially, and `D Jλ=D`. If its Gram matrix were zero, `Jλ²=0`, contradicting `D Jλ²=D`. Choose u with `D c_uu^λ≠0` or, more generally, a nonzero `d c_su^λ`; multiplying by `c_uv^λ` produces the right cell row. Its span is a quotient of Cλ that is all of D by simplicity. Since every proper submodule of this nonzero-form Cλ lies in Rλ, that simple quotient is Dλ. For the general off-diagonal choice, first choose s,u,d with `d c_su≠0`; the map `c_v↦d c_sv` is the cell-row map and has nonzero image. This proves all simple labels without classifying which multipartitions have nonzero forms.

The order and distinctness follow directly from the ideals. Cλ annihilates Iµ whenever λ does not dominate µ: products in `Iλ∩Iµ` have only shapes strictly above λ in this case. Dµ does not annihilate Iµ because its rank-one action is nonzero. Hence `[Cλ:Dµ]≠0` implies λ dominates µ. Rλ annihilates Iλ by the rank-one action, while Dλ does not, so `[Cλ:Dλ]=1`. Distinct nonzero heads cannot be isomorphic: their ideal supports would force both λ≥µ and µ≥λ. This proves the complete split simple-label and triangular multiplicity statements over every F.

## 2. Each cell module belongs to a single block, even if its form is zero

Let z be a central idempotent of A. On the cell layer `Jλ≅(Cλ)^*⊗_F Cλ`, equality of left and right multiplication by z gives `B⊗Id=Id⊗Aλ`, where B and Aλ are its first- and second-factor coefficient matrices. Choose bases in both factors and compare matrix coefficients. Every off-diagonal coefficient of B and Aλ is zero, and every diagonal coefficient of either equals every diagonal coefficient of the other. Thus both are one scalar θλ times the identity. Since z is idempotent, θλ is0 or1. This tensor argument does not divide by the Gram matrix and still works when it is identically zero.

Apply it to all primitive central idempotents, whose sum is1. Exactly one acts as1 on the nonzero cell module Cλ, the others as0. Thus Cλ and every composition factor of it belong to one block. This proves the cell-purity claim required for all Specht modules, including labels with Dλ=0.

## 3. The exact shared-cell-factor linkage criterion

Because the simples are absolutely split and self-dual under * (their nonsingular quotient forms identify each with its contragredient), choose one primitive idempotent eµ for each simple Dµ with `dim Dν eµ=δµν`. The exact functor `V↦V eµ` gives `dim Cλ eµ=[Cλ:Dµ]=dλµ`; the corresponding left-factor dimension is the same after applying *. Filter A by a linear extension of its cellular ideals and apply `eµ(-)eν`. The cell layer is the outer tensor product of its two cell modules. Exactness and dimension additivity therefore give

`dim_F eµ A eν=Σ_λ dλµ dλν`.

No multiplicity computation is hidden in this identity. Projecting with an idempotent is exact: for a surjection lift a vector and multiply the lift by the idempotent; for an injection restrict it. The same reasoning gives exactness for the two-sided projection.

A finite split algebra's blocks are the connected components of its primitive-idempotent corner graph: put an edge whenever `e A f` or `f A e` is nonzero. For a union of graph components, the sum of its full primitive idempotents commutes with every corner of A and is central. Conversely, a central block idempotent is0 or1 on each primitive idempotent and cannot separate a nonzero corner. These two statements prove the graph characterization; repeated primitive idempotents for the same simple are linked because their matrix units survive in the semisimple quotient.

The displayed Cartan identity says that two simple labels have a nonzero corner exactly when they occur together as factors of some cell module. Consequently two simples lie in the same block exactly when a finite chain of cell modules links their factors. Since every cell module is pure and every simple occurs in a nonzero-form cell head, two cell modules lie in the same block exactly when there is a chain of cell modules with each neighboring pair sharing a simple composition factor. This is the exact typed shared-standard/Specht linkage criterion; it is not inferred for arbitrary unrelated modules.

items.title: Selfadjoint weight Gram valuations detect integer Jantzen classes
items.statement:
In Leaf A suppose 1=sum_nu e_nu is a finite decomposition into pairwise orthogonal idempotents of A, with e_nu*=e_nu. Write M_nu=e_nu M and G_nu for the restricted Gram matrix. Then each M_nu is finite free, each restricted generic form is nondegenerate, and

$$\sum_{s>0}\dim_F e_\nu M_F^s=\nu_\pi(\det G_\nu).$$

For a split finite-dimensional highest-weight algebra S_F whose standard classes [Delta(mu)] form a Z-basis of K0, if the matrix K_{mu nu}=dim e_nu Delta(mu) has a square unitriangular submatrix indexed by partition weights, then the weight-character map ch:K0 -> Z^{weights}, [N] -> (dim e_nu N)_nu is injective. It follows that a class equality involving Jantzen pieces is equivalent to the corresponding equalities of weight Gram valuations.

**Statement.** In Leaf A suppose 1=sum_nu e_nu is a finite decomposition into pairwise orthogonal idempotents of A, with e_nu*=e_nu. Write M_nu=e_nu M and G_nu for the restricted Gram matrix. Then each M_nu is finite free, each restricted generic form is nondegenerate, and

$$\sum_{s>0}\dim_F e_\nu M_F^s=\nu_\pi(\det G_\nu).$$

For a split finite-dimensional highest-weight algebra S_F whose standard classes [Delta(mu)] form a Z-basis of K0, if the matrix K_{mu nu}=dim e_nu Delta(mu) has a square unitriangular submatrix indexed by partition weights, then the weight-character map ch:K0 -> Z^{weights}, [N] -> (dim e_nu N)_nu is injective. It follows that a class equality involving Jantzen pieces is equivalent to the corresponding equalities of weight Gram valuations.

**Proof.** The decomposition M=sum e_nu M is direct, and each summand is a direct summand of a finite free O-module, hence free: choose generators, use the preceding DVR elimination on the inclusion, or the fact that a submodule of a finite free module over the DVR is free. For nu!=rho, b(e_nu x,e_rho y)=b(x,e_nu e_rho y)=0. A vector in M_nu,K orthogonal to its summand is orthogonal to all summands and is zero by generic nondegeneracy. Thus the restricted form is nondegenerate. Orthogonality gives M(s)=direct sum M_nu(s), and reduction respects this direct sum. Leaf A applied to M_nu proves the displayed equality.

Each functor N -> e_nu N is exact: injectivity and kernels follow by restriction, and a lift of y=e_nu y in a quotient can be replaced by e_nu x. Thus ch is additive and defined on K0. Write an element as sum_mu a_mu[Delta(mu)]. Its coordinates on the partition weights are the integer row vector a multiplied by a unitriangular matrix K. This matrix is invertible over Z by finite triangular elimination. If the character is zero, a=0. Apply this injectivity to sum_s [Delta(lambda)^s] - sum_mu J_{lambda mu}[Delta(mu)] and use the valuation equality just proved. No Schur functor, residue-sequence character, rationalization, or semisimple Hecke Grothendieck group is used.

items.title: A symmetric-polynomial center makes split content idempotents primitive
items.statement: Let A be a finite-dimensional unital F-algebra, with commuting elements x_1,...,x_d and split joint regular-module generalized-eigenprojectors p_word∈A, pairwise orthogonal and summing to1, with (x_r−word_r)p_word nilpotent. For each finite multiset α of eigenvalues let eα be the sum over words of that multiset, and assume each eα is central. If Z(A) is the image of the symmetric polynomial ring in x_1,...,x_d, then each eα is zero or primitive central, and its nonzero terms are exactly all primitive central idempotents of A. No splitting-simple-module or algebraically closed field hypothesis is required. For d=0 the asserted symmetric-center hypothesis says Z(A)=F·1 and yields the same conclusion.
items.strategy:
**Given:** the finite commuting split-projector family and the stated symmetric-center equality. Write n=d; if n=0 the center is F·1 and its only idempotents are0,1, so below let n≥1. In each content summand the projector decomposition is a decomposition of its regular vector space, so an element nilpotent on every one of its finitely many projector summands is nilpotent there. Use this in the following full local-center proof.

Fix nonzero e=eα. For 1≤k≤n let σk be the kth elementary symmetric polynomial. Let ak be its value on a word of content α; this is independent of word order. On each p_word A inside eA write xᵢ=wordᵢ+Nᵢ, with commuting nilpotent Nᵢ. A polynomial in the Nᵢ with zero constant term is nilpotent: if Nᵢ^M=0 for all i, any product of more than n(M−1) positive-degree monomials vanishes. Hence

Nk=eσk(x)−ak e

is nilpotent on every word summand. There are only finitely many words, so some common exponent makes Nk zero in eA. The Nk commute; the ideal J they generate in the commutative ring eZ(A) is nilpotent by the same degree count.

Every symmetric polynomial is a polynomial in σ₁,…,σₙ over F. This elementary symmetric-polynomial theorem is characteristic free: subtract the product of elementary polynomials with matching largest monomial, and iterate in lexicographic order. The assumed symmetric-center equality therefore gives eZ(A)=F e+J. Since e≠0 and J is nilpotent, F e∩J=0, and eZ(A)/J≅F. An idempotent z in this ring has image 0 or 1 in F. In the first case z∈J is both nilpotent and idempotent, hence z=0. In the second e−z is both nilpotent and idempotent, hence z=e. Thus e is primitive central.

Since the eα are central, pairwise orthogonal, and sum to 1, their nonzero terms are exactly all primitive central idempotents: for another primitive central b, the decomposition b=Σα beα has exactly one nonzero term; that term equals eα because eα is primitive. Every block therefore arises from exactly one nonzero eα. No algebraic closure, splitting-simple-module theorem, power-sum generation, division by n!, or level-one restriction is used.

items.strategy:
# Finite cyclotomic Hecke algebras and spectral propagation

Research construction for the native24 first repair. This is an actual algebraic route for the finite/split-spectral input of the CRT definition. It does not claim the stronger bounded ordered-monomial basis or content-idempotent primitivity. Those retained claims have separate construction obligations. No native readiness or independent audit is claimed.

Fix the native affine presentations, an arbitrary field F, finite quantum characteristic e≥2, dominant Λ and the standard split FIRST cyclotomic polynomial. Put ℓ=Σ_i λ_i. The DG branch has q=1 and charF=e, the NG branch q≠1 and q has order e. At d=0 use HΛ_0=F. At d>0 with ℓ=0 the first relation is1=0, so the algebra is zero; below assumeℓ>0.

1. **Normal spanning, without a cyclotomic basis assumption.** The DG mixed relation lets each polynomial generator pass each simple reflection, with its permutation term and a scalar lower term. In NG the relations give
   X_r T_r=T_r X_(r+1)+(1-q)X_(r+1),
   X_(r+1) T_r=T_r X_r+(q-1)X_(r+1),
   and the inverse-variable versions printed immediately after BK(4.5). Solve these equations in the opposite direction to move every Laurent variable left. All correction terms have fewer misplaced variable/crossing pairs, so induction terminates. The image of the finite Hecke subalgebra is spanned by the images of T_w, by its existing standard-basis supplier (only its spanning clause is consumed, no injectivity in the affine algebra is assumed). Thus affine ordered polynomial/Laurent monomials times T_w span. For DG use the group-algebra image and its finite permutation basis. This is enough here; independence is not used.

2. **Global intertwiners from the presentation.** For neighboring polynomial variables x,y, the DG element θ=s(x-y)+1 satisfies θx=yθ and θ²=1-(x-y)². For NG commuting units x,y, Θ=T(1-xy^(-1))+1-q satisfies Θx=yΘ and Θ²=(x-qy)(y-qx)/(xy). These are identities in the WHOLE affine algebra, without spectral idempotents or unequal-color inverse differences. Substitute the mixed equation s y=x s+1 and s²=1 for DG. For NG substitute T²=(q-1)T+q and TxT=qy, using T^(-1)=q^(-1)T+q^(-1)-1. Expanding the two squares and moving variables gives exactly the displayed products. Hence they remain valid in the quotient. These are the global identities BK(3.10)–(3.12), (4.10)–(4.12), whose full proof-bearing presentation and uses were read; the algebraic substitutions are reproduced here rather than importing the foreign spectral lemma.

3. **Monic propagation via a finite power-basis norm.** Suppose a split monic f(x) annihilates the old variable. Then θ f(x) θ=f(y) θ²=0, or Θ f(x) Θ=f(y) Θ²=0. In DG this says f(y)[1-(x-y)²]=0. In NG multiply by the commuting unitxy to get f(y)(x-qy)(y-qx)=0. Let C=F[z]/f(z), with its explicit basis1,z,...,z^(D-1), D=degf. Multiplication by the respective quadratic r(z,y) on C[y] has matrix M(y) with leading coefficient -Id (DG) or -qId (NG), hence detM(y) has invertible leading coefficient. The adjugate identity, applied to the basis vector1, writes r(z,y)R(z,y)=detM(y) in C[y]. Lift back to F[x,y], multiply by f(y), and use f(x)=0 and f(y)r(x,y)=0. It follows that f(y)detM(y)=0. Divide by its leading scalar to obtain a monic next-variable annihilator. No flatness, algebraic closure, generic faithfulness or denominator difference is assumed.

4. **Spectral inclusion.** If f(z)=∏_a(z-a) with multiplicities, the same power-basis determinant has product ∏_a r(a,y), since its multiplication matrix is triangular after the finite decomposition into factors (or by the companion-matrix resultant identity). In DG its new roots are a+1,a-1; in NG they are qa,q^(-1)a. Thus starting from ∏_i(x_1-i)^λ_i gives roots entirely in the prime-field residue set; starting from ∏_i(X_1-q^i)^λ_i gives roots in{q^i}. Both sets are closed under the indicated moves. Multiplicities are retained; no square-free assumption is made. In NG all roots remain nonzero, so every annihilator has nonzero constant coefficient. Its monic relation expresses the inverse variable as a polynomial in that variable.

5. **Finiteness and canonical CRT projectors.** Apply the construction successively along the positions. Each polynomial variable has a finite-degree monic annihilator, so normal spanning reduces its exponents below this degree, with negative exponents eliminated in NG. Finitely many exponent tuples and T_w span HΛ_d. This proves finite dimension without the exact ℓ^d d! basis theorem. The minimal polynomial on its regular module divides the constructed split annihilator; consequently it has only the required eigenvalues. The usual finite polynomial Euclidean/CRT construction gives the canonical projectors ε_r(i), including zero factors. Their commuting products e(i) sum to1 and act on every finite module as the corresponding simultaneous generalized-eigenspace projectors. This proves precisely the needed spectral/finite input of the native residue definition over the actual original field. Centrality follows from the local Hecke cross/intertwiner identities, independently of primitivity: the only possible image of an i-weight under the neighboring Hecke generator has weightsi ands_r i, so fixed-content sums are invariant. Primitivity is NOT inferred from this argument.

This lemma consumes only the native affine presentation and the choice-free finite Hecke standard-spanning clause. It is independent of the blockwise BK isomorphism, the cyclotomic exact-dimension theorem, the primitive-content theorem, and all global-basis claims. The separated logical route prevents those later claims from being used to establish their own prerequisites.

items.title: Charged core matrices admit size descent and minimum-size switch connectivity
items.statement: Fix finite $e\ge2$, $\ell\ge1$ and charges $c_a\in\mathbb Z$. Give nodes of component $a$ residue $c_a+j-i\pmod e$. Write $C_i$ for residue counts and $\delta_i$ for removable minus addable $i$-nodes. Then $\delta_i=2C_i-C_{i-1}-C_{i+1}-m_i$, $m_i=\#\{a:c_a\equiv i\}$, with both neighboring terms retained at $e=2$. Equal hubs and equal size are equivalent to equal content. For componentwise $e$-cores, let $b_{ia}$ be the largest charged beta bead on runner $i$ and $t_{ia}=(b_{ia}-i)/e$. Cores of fixed hub/charges correspond exactly to integer matrices with fixed row sums and column sums $c_a-e$; for two such cores, their size difference is $\frac e2$ times the difference of $\sum t_{ia}^2$. Every nonminimum-size core admits a finite same-hub core-switch path that never increases size and ends at a smaller core. Every pair of minimum-size cores is connected by equal-size switches. A switch subtracts1 at $(i,a),(j,b)$ and adds1 at $(i,b),(j,a)$; each path switch can be oriented with $\gamma=t_{ia}-t_{ib}-t_{ja}+t_{jb}\ge2$, giving size change $-e(\gamma-2)$. Minimum cores exist for every nonempty fixed-hub class.
items.strategy:
**Given:** the charged beta/core conventions and [[lem-ultra-tight-multisets-admit-column-potentials]].

Fix e≥2, ℓ≥1 and integer charges c₁,…,cℓ. A component λ^(a) has beta set Bₐ={λ_i^(a)+cₐ−i:i≥1}. It contains all sufficiently negative integers and no sufficiently positive integers, and for large N it has N+cₐ elements ≥−N. Conversely every such set gives a partition: order its elements β₁>β₂>⋯ and put λ_i=β_i−cₐ+i. These integers are decreasing, eventually zero, and therefore nonnegative.

A bead move u→u−h, where u∈B and u−h∉B, unwraps a rim hook of length h with foot residue u−h+1 modulo e. This can be checked directly: if β_i=u and β_j<u−h<β_(j−1), the rows i through j−1 change by the shifted boundary between those two beta positions; the lost border strip has h boxes. Its lowest row is j−1 and its leftmost lost column there is (u−h)−cₐ+j, so its foot content is u−h+1. Reversing the move wraps the hook with foot residue its starting beta position plus one. In particular moving a bead upward one position on its runner removes an e-hook. Repeating packs every runner upwards. The result is independent of removal order because the number of beads relative to the negative reference tail on each runner is preserved. The packed component is its e-core. Every e-hook contains one node of each residue, so hook removal leaves the hub invariant and subtracts the all-one vector from the residue counts.

Let Cᵢ(λ) be node residue counts and mᵢ=#{a:cₐ≡i mod e}. Set δᵢ=number of removable i-nodes minus number of addable i-nodes. We have

δᵢ=2Cᵢ−Cᵢ₋₁−Cᵢ₊₁−mᵢ, with cyclic indices (the two neighboring terms coincide and occur twice if e=2).

One direct proof is induction while adjoining nodes: the empty multipartition has δᵢ=−mᵢ; adjoining a node of residue j changes the boundary count by +2 at j and −1 at each of j−1,j+1, counted twice when e=2. These changes follow by recording the occupied/vacant beta positions before and after the one-position bead move; all other adjacent occupancies cancel. The residue-count expression changes in exactly the same way. This also derives Fayers weight-paper Lemmas 2.3 and 3.1 without a Lie-theoretic assumption.

If two multipartitions have equal hubs, their residue-count difference d satisfies 2dᵢ−dᵢ₋₁−dᵢ₊₁=0. Thus the first differences dᵢ−dᵢ₋₁ are all equal; summing them around the cycle makes this common difference zero. Therefore d is constant. Consequently equal hub and equal size imply equal content; equal hubs imply sizes congruent modulo e.

For a component core let bᵢₐ be the largest bead on runner i, 0≤i<e, and define the integer

tᵢₐ=(bᵢₐ−i)/e.

The packed beta set on runner i is {i+ek:k≤tᵢₐ}. The column sums satisfy Σᵢtᵢₐ=cₐ−e, by counting beads ≥−eL for large L. Writing Rᵢ=Σₐtᵢₐ, the hub satisfies δᵢ=Rᵢ−Rᵢ₋₁ for 1≤i<e and δ₀=R₀−R_(e−1)−ℓ. Since ΣᵢRᵢ=Σₐcₐ−eℓ is fixed, equal hub is equivalent to equal row sums. Thus cores of a fixed hub and charges are exactly integer e×ℓ matrices with fixed row and column sums.

If κ,η are such cores, then

|η|−|κ|=(e/2)(Σᵢₐtᵢₐ(η)²−Σᵢₐtᵢₐ(κ)²).

To prove it, count beta numbers ≥−eL in each component. Their number is eL+cₐ, the same for both cores. Their sum changes by Σᵢ i Δtᵢₐ+(e/2)ΣᵢΔ(tᵢₐ²+tᵢₐ). From β_j=λ_j+cₐ−j, the change in this sum equals the change in partition size. Sum over a: equal row sums kill Σᵢ iΣₐΔtᵢₐ, and equal margins kill the linear ΣΔt term. This proves the formula. In particular the squared-norm difference is even, so the displayed expression is an integer multiple of e.

Use the column-potential lemma just cited in the following finite energy argument.

Let T=(tᵢₐ) be an integer e×ℓ matrix with fixed margins. A switch in distinct rows i,j and distinct columns a,b replaces

(tᵢₐ,tᵢ_b,tⱼₐ,tⱼ_b) by (tᵢₐ−1,tᵢ_b+1,tⱼₐ+1,tⱼ_b−1).

Put γ=tᵢₐ−tᵢ_b−tⱼₐ+tⱼ_b. Its squared-norm change is 4−2γ. Hence γ=2 is a zero-energy switch and γ≥3 strictly decreases energy. Regard the e labeled rows of T as a multiset in L_ℓ. They are tight exactly when every γ≤2; switches with γ=2 are exactly zero exchanges.

If the row multiset is not ultra-tight, a finite sequence of zero switches leads to a non-tight matrix. There γ≥3 for some rows and columns, giving a strict descent. Every intermediate matrix has the same margins, and the descent lowers core size by e(γ−2), while zero switches preserve it.

If it is ultra-tight, the lemma provides a column potential sₐ such that each row of U=(tᵢₐ−sₐ) has maximum minus minimum at most one. For a fixed integer row sum, such a row minimizes the sum of squares over all integer rows: if entries differ by ≥2, transferring one from the larger to the smaller lowers the square sum by at least two; repeated transfers terminate. Its minimum is achieved exactly by rows whose entries differ by at most one. Column potentials do not affect comparisons of total squared norm between matrices with the same column sums, since

Σ(tᵢₐ−sₐ)²=Σtᵢₐ²−2ΣₐsₐΣᵢtᵢₐ+eΣₐsₐ².

Thus T is a global minimum among matrices of its margins. Conversely a global minimum cannot admit a strict descent after zero switches, so its row multiset is ultra-tight. Starting from any T, repeated zero-path/strict-descent steps reach a global minimum: all matrices represent genuine cores of nonnegative integer size, and strict descent lowers that size by at least e.

Now let T,V be two global minima of the same margins. Use the column potential s of T. Every row of U=T−s is balanced, say its entries are uᵢ or uᵢ+1. Since V−s has the same row sums and the same total energy, each of its rows also attains the row minimum and therefore has entries uᵢ or uᵢ+1. Subtract uᵢ from row i. We obtain two binary e×ℓ matrices A,B with identical row and column sums.

Here is a complete binary-switch connectivity proof (Fayers Proposition 2.4, author PDF pp.15–16). If A≠B, write D=A−B. Its nonzero entries are ±1, with all row and column sums zero. Starting at a +1, alternate a −1 in its row and a +1 in that column. A repeated location gives an alternating cycle. Choose a shortest such cycle, with distinct rows i₀,…,i_(t−1) and columns j₀,…,j_(t−1), where D_(i_k,j_k)=+1 and D_(i_k,j_(k+1))=−1, cyclically. If t=2, switch its rectangle in A to agree with B there. If t>2 inspect A_(i₀,j_(t−1)) and B_(i₀,j_(t−1)). If A there is 0, switching the rectangle with rows i₀,i_(t−1) and columns j₀,j_(t−1) gives a binary A' and strictly fewer discrepancies with B. If B there is 1, the reverse switch on B gives a binary B' with strictly fewer discrepancies with A. If neither condition holds, D there is +1 and a shorter alternating cycle exists, contradicting minimality. Induct on the discrepancy count; every binary switch preserves margins. Hence A and B are connected by binary switches.

Lifting these binary switches to T gives switches with γ=2 and thus preserves core size and hub. Therefore any two minimum-size cores of a given hub and fixed charges are connected by equal-size elementary core switches. Any nonminimum core admits a core-switch path that preserves hub, never increases size, and ends at strictly smaller size. These are exactly the finite-e descent and reduced-core connectivity facts consumed by the Lyle–Mathas max-weight argument. This proves F locally without Fayers' weight nonnegativity, pairwise-weight formula, or matrix-alignment Proposition 2.5 as additional inputs.

items.title: Ordinary type-A permutation modules have semistandard Murphy bases and Specht filtrations
items.statement: For every commutative ring R, invertible z, ordinary finite type-A Hecke algebra H_n and composition ρ of n, xρH_n has R-basis m_(S,t)=Σ_(s:ρ(s)=S)m_st for semistandard partition-shape S of typeρ and standard t of the same shape. It has a Specht filtration with multiplicity #SStdρ(λ) of the ordinary Specht Sλ. The row-double-coset membership uses each coset word once and no quantum-factorial division. Over the generic field this number equals the trivial-character multiplicity of the ρ-row parabolic in Sλ. The explicit ordinary Garnir row-coset identity, additive nonstandard-tableau factorization, and same-column generator refinement T_a m_st≡−m_st+Σ_(u⊲s)c_u m_ut modulo higher shapes hold; row-standard straightening has no smaller-shape terms and its same-shape terms increase tableau-prefix dominance. Shape support uses the already proved ordinary Murphy dominance ideals; the finite Garnir algorithm terminates in lexicographic shape/tableau order before that dominance refinement.
items.strategy:
This is the narrow ordinary type-A supplier actually needed by Q-S1's finite Mackey count. It is stated separately so that the higher-level theorem does not pretend that a definition of the ordinary Schur algebra supplies its proof. Inputs are the ordinary finite-Hecke standard and Murphy bases/cell law, including the explicit ordinary Garnir construction below. Everything is over a commutative ring with invertible z; prove the coefficient statements first universally over Z[z,z^-1].

Let ρ be a composition of n, xρ its row symmetrizer, and µ a partition shape. For ordinary semistandard S of shapeµ/typeρ and standard t of shapeµ set `m_(S,t)=Σ_(s:ρ(s)=S)m_st`. Then these sums are an R-basis of `xρ H`; ordering them by higher shape first yields a Specht filtration with one copy of Sµ for every such S.

The finite row-double-coset identity gives exact membership. Every row-standard refinement of column-strict S is standard, so `Σ_s T_d(s)* xµ` is the sum of T_w over the double coset `Sρ d(s0)^-1 Sµ`, each w exactly once. Its left Sρ-coset expansion writes it as `xρ h0`. Appending T_d(t) gives `m_(S,t)=xρ h`. No row-intersection quantum factorial is introduced. The sums are independent since their Murphy fibres are disjoint and all coefficients are1.

We spell out the column refinement used in the coefficient argument. In the ordinary Garnir proof, for a violation at adjacent rows i,i+1 and column j, use the composition `ν=(µ_1,...,µ_(i-1),j-1,µ_i+1,µ_(i+1)-j,µ_(i+2),...)`. The two length-additive coset sums of `Sν Sµ` give

`Σ_(w∈Sν∩Dµ)xµT_w=Σ_(v∈Sµ∩Dν)T_v* xν`.

Its distinguished Garnir term occurs with coefficient1. All other terms in its original shape have strictly more dominant row tableaux; the reordered ν has strictly higher lexicographic shape, and the ordinary Murphy dominance refinement puts these shape errors in higher-cell ideals. A nonstandard tableau factors as that Garnir tableau followed by an additive-length word, obtained by removing inversions while keeping the column violation. Bruhat subword support preserves the strict tableau-prefix inequality on multiplication by that word. When the entries in the offending column are consecutive a,a+1, sorting the Garnir belt has a unique standard term whose single adjacent swap produces its distinguished Garnir term; its coefficient in the isolated relation is−1. Every other same-shape term is strictly more dominant. This proves, after the ordinary dominance refinement,

`T_a m_st ≡ -m_st+Σ_(u⊲s)c_u m_ut (mod higher shapes)`

whenever a,a+1 occupy one column of s. The right analogue follows by *. In contrast, if `s s_a` is standard, length/quadratic multiplication gives exactly the two usual swapped-tableau terms, with no shape error; if they occupy one row it gives exactly z m_st. These are the complete local finite-generator rules used below.

For a fixed a, the left z-eigenspace of T_a in the finite Hecke algebra is `(1+T_a)H`. Indeed in the T_w basis, pair w and s_aw with the latter of larger length; coefficient comparison in `T_a h=z h` gives equality of their two coefficients. Their sum is `(1+T_a)T_w`. This argument uses z as a unit, not z+1 as a unit.

Over the universal domain, no element of this row eigenspace has a nonzero Murphy coefficient at a tableau with a,a+1 in one column. To prove this, choose a least shape and then a least left tableau in a dominance-compatible support order. Higher-cell terms cannot contribute to its shape and a column correction from another tableau can contribute only from a strictly less dominant left tableau, absent by minimality. If its a,a+1 are in a column, its coefficient in `T_a h` is the negative of its coefficient in h, contradicting the z-eigenvalue equation because z+1 is nonzero in the domain. If they share a row, its basis element is itself a z-eigenvector, hence belongs to the row ideal by the preceding standard-basis test; subtract its coefficient times that element. If their swap is standard, the coefficient equation at the less dominant of the pair makes the two coefficients equal, and their sum is a z-eigenvector by the exact two-tableau rules. Subtract this common coefficient times the pair. Each subtraction stays in the row ideal and removes at least the chosen support term without creating any new support term. Induction on the finite support eliminates it and proves the asserted column exclusion. Specializing the resulting coordinate-zero identities for the standard row-ideal generators proves the same assertion over every base ring; no cancellation of z+1 at a singular parameter is used.

Now h∈xρH is a z-eigenvector for every generator inside every ρ-row interval. The column exclusion applies for each consecutive pair inside such an interval. Consequently every supported tableau has those pairs in different columns. For an adjacent swap that is standard, comparison of the exact two-tableau coefficient equations gives equality of its two coefficients; column-state correction terms cannot interfere, because every such state has coefficient0 by the just-proved exclusion.

The standard refinements of a fixed row-label tableau are linear extensions of the finite node posets within its repeated-label classes. Two extensions are connected by swaps of adjacent incomparable elements: moving the first differing desired element left across its preceding incomparable elements reduces their inversion distance, and finite induction proves connectivity. If a repeated label occupies one column, an adjacent vertical cover in that repeated-label subposet can be consecutive in some extension; contract that cover, take any finite topological order, and expand the contracted element as its two endpoints. Thus valid adjacent swaps carry its coefficient to one excluded consecutive-column state, and the whole fibre has coefficient0. Otherwise the row-label tableau is column-strict, and every fibre coefficient is one common coefficient. This proves that h has zero coefficients off semistandard fibres and constant coefficients on every semistandard fibre, hence lies in the span of the sums. Exact membership and disjoint unit pivots prove the basis theorem.

Finally, order semistandard S's in a linear extension of shape dominance. The Murphy cell law preserves the corresponding higher-shape filtration. For a fixed S the action on the vectors m_(S,t) modulo higher terms is the ordinary Specht action, since its coefficients do not depend on the left refinement. Thus the successive quotients are the stated Specht modules. Over the generic field, finite-Hecke semisimplicity makes their multiplicities equal to the trivial-character multiplicities under the ρ-row parabolic by induction/restriction adjunction. This is exactly the ordinary number consumed in the higher-level Mackey count.


For the generic finite-Hecke assertion, ordinary JM words distinguish tableaux across all partition shapes by their successive addable-node contents. By [[lem-finite-cellular-nonzero-form-heads-purity-and-shared-factor-linkage]], every simple is a nonzero cellular head. A simple factor of an ordinary cell module has a word character from that module and from the head’s own cell shape; disjoint word sets force that same shape. Existence of a factor forces its own head nonzero, and diagonal multiplicity1 forces the cell module simple. The sum of their squared dimensions equals the finite-Hecke rank, so the generic algebra and each parabolic are split semisimple. This supplies the generic multiplicity premise locally.

items.title: Level-one cyclotomic Hecke algebras are the finite Hecke algebras
items.statement: Let $\Lambda=\Lambda_j$ be a level-one fundamental weight and keep the conventions of [[def-type-a-affine-presentations-and-charged-cyclotomic-quotients]]. Then the assignments $T_r\mapsto T_r$ ($1\le r<d$) in the nondegenerate case and $s_r\mapsto s_r$ in the degenerate case extend to $F$-algebra isomorphisms $H_{F,q}(S_d)\to H^\Lambda_d$ and $FS_d\to H^\Lambda_d$ respectively.
items.strategy: At level one the first polynomial forces X_1=q_H^j (NG) or x_1=j (DG). Recurrence expresses every subsequent polynomial generator in the finite generators, so the standard finite-Hecke/group map is surjective. Construct its inverse without dimensions: in NG let L_r be the ordinary additive JM element, M_r=1+(q_H−1)L_r=q_H^(1−r)T_(r−1)⋯T_1^2⋯T_(r−1), and set X_r=q_H^j M_r. The ordinary JM elements commute, each M_r is a product of units, and T_r M_r T_r=q_H M_(r+1); distant mixed commutation follows from their finite words. These elements satisfy the complete affine relations and X_1=q_H^j. In DG set x_r=j+Σ_(a<r)(a r); direct transposition multiplication gives commuting JM elements, s_r x_(r+1)=x_r s_r+1 and distant commutation. Both constructions satisfy the first polynomial and define inverse homomorphisms fixing the finite generators, hence mutual inverses on every presentation generator. Rank zero is F. This removes the late-basis/dimension dependency and introduces no BK or primitive-block input.

items.title: The affine and cyclotomic type-A Hecke algebras
items.statement:
Let $F$ be a field and $q\in F^{\times}$ with FINITE quantum characteristic $e=e(F,q)$, $2\le e<\infty$, residue set $I=\mathbb Z/e\mathbb Z$ with integer residue labels $0,1,\dots,e-1$; in the nondegenerate branch their distinct spectral values are $q^i$, while in the degenerate branch they are $i\cdot1_F$ (here $e=\operatorname{char}F$), and the cyclic affine type-A Cartan datum with dominant weights $P^+$ and pairing $(\Lambda,\alpha_i)$ ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]], [[def-cyclic-affine-type-a-cartan-datum]]). Fix $\Lambda\in P^+$ of level $\ell=\sum_{i\in I}(\Lambda,\alpha_i)$ and put $\lambda_i:=(\Lambda,\alpha_i)$.

**(NG) Nondegenerate case $q\ne1$.** The affine Hecke algebra of type $A_{d-1}$ at parameter $q$ is the unital $F$-algebra $H_d$ with generators $X_1^{\pm1},\dots,X_d^{\pm1}$, $T_1,\dots,T_{d-1}$ and relations (4.2)-(4.5) of the source: $X_rX_s=X_sX_r$, $X_rX_r^{-1}=1$, $T_rX_rT_r=qX_{r+1}$, $T_rX_s=X_sT_r$ ($s\notin\{r,r+1\}$), $T_r^2=(q-1)T_r+q$, $T_rT_{r+1}T_r=T_{r+1}T_rT_{r+1}$, $T_rT_s=T_sT_r$ ($|r-s|>1$). The **cyclotomic Hecke algebra** is $H^\Lambda_d:=H_d/\langle\prod_{i\in I}(X_1-q^i)^{\lambda_i}\rangle$.

**(DG) Degenerate case $q=1$** (then necessarily $\operatorname{char}F=e>0$). The **degenerate affine Hecke algebra** $H_d$ is the unital $F$-algebra with generators $x_1,\dots,x_d,s_1,\dots,s_{d-1}$ and relations (3.2)-(3.5): $x_rx_s=x_sx_r$, $s_rx_{r+1}=x_rs_r+1$, $s_rx_s=x_ss_r$ ($s\notin\{r,r+1\}$), $s_r^2=1$, braid and distant commutation; its ordered monomials $x_1^{m_1}\cdots x_d^{m_d}w$ form an $F$-basis by [[lem-degenerate-affine-hecke-ordered-monomials-form-a-basis]]. The **degenerate cyclotomic Hecke algebra** is $H^\Lambda_d:=H_d/\langle\prod_{i\in I}(x_1-i)^{\lambda_i}\rangle$.

**Conventions.** $H^\Lambda_0=F$; the cyclotomic polynomial is imposed on the FIRST polynomial generator; $T_r$ acts on positions $r,r+1$. The Hecke parameter is the one of [[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]] ($T_i^2=(q-1)T_i+q$). At level one $\Lambda=\Lambda_j$, $H^\Lambda_d$ is the finite type-A Hecke algebra $H_{F,q}(S_d)$ if $q\ne1$ and the group algebra $FS_d$ if $q=1$ ([[prop-cyclotomic-hecke-algebras-of-level-one-are-finite-hecke-algebras]]). Only finite $e$ is treated: the source's $e=0$ branches ($q$ not a root of unity, and the characteristic-zero degeneration, whose quiver is $A_\infty$) are outside this page's cyclic scope and are deferred in the batch notes. No choice principle is used.
items.strategy: The pure presentations and charged quotients are [[def-type-a-affine-presentations-and-charged-cyclotomic-quotients]]. The required field-independent DG ordered basis is the declared local rational-operator/Bruhat-leading proof, not an unconsumed batch17 realization. The level-one fact is proved independently by the explicit JM inverse in the declared proposition. Integer I labels produce distinct spectral values q_H^i in NG and i·1_F in DG; no impossible NG embedding of I into F is used. The original finite-e scope and source normalization are retained.

items.title: The type-A cyclotomic specialization of the KLR algebras
items.statement: Let $F,q,e,I,\Lambda,\lambda_i$ be as in [[def-affine-and-cyclotomic-type-a-hecke-algebras]]. On the cyclic affine type-A Cartan datum define the normalized symmetrizers d_i=1 and the type-A KLR datum $Q^{A}$ by $Q^{A}_{ii}=0$, $Q^{A}_{ij}=1$ if $a_{ij}=0$, $Q^{A}_{i,i+1}(u,v)=v-u$ and $Q^{A}_{i+1,i}(u,v)=u-v$ for the two edge orientations when $e\ge3$, and $Q^{A}_{01}(u,v)=Q^{A}_{10}(u,v)=-(u-v)^2$ when $e=2$. Then $Q^{A}$ satisfies (Q1)-(Q4) of [[def-quiver-hecke-klr-algebra-for-a-symmetrizable-cartan-datum]]. Write $R_\alpha$ for the resulting generalised KLR algebra over $F$ and $R^\Lambda_\alpha$ for the STANDARD cyclotomic quotient of [[def-cyclotomic-klr-quotient-at-a-dominant-weight]] (monic first-strand relations $x_1^{\lambda_{i_1}}e(\nu)=0$). With $y_r:=x_r$ and $\psi_r:=-\tau_r$ the relations (1.6)-(1.15) of the source hold in $R^\Lambda_\alpha$, and conversely the quotient presented by those relations is the same algebra; in other words $R^\Lambda_\alpha$ is the sign-modified cyclotomic Khovanov-Lauda algebra of the source for the cyclic quiver of quantum characteristic $e$.
items.strategy:

items.title: Intertwining elements and the local power-series calculus in a cyclotomic Hecke block
items.statement: Let $H^\Lambda_\alpha$ be a central content sector (possibly zero) as in [[def-cyclotomic-hecke-central-content-sector-notation]]. (i) Set $y_r:=\sum_{i\in I_\alpha}(x_r-i_r)e(i)$ in the degenerate case and $y_r:=\sum_{i\in I_\alpha}(1-q^{-i_r}X_r)e(i)$ in the nondegenerate case ($1\le r\le d$). Then $y_1,\dots,y_d$ are commuting nilpotent elements of $H^\Lambda_\alpha$; consequently every rational expression displayed below, expanded as a power series in the nilpotent $y$'s, is a finite and well-defined element of $H^\Lambda_\alpha$. (ii) The power series $p_r(i):=1$ if $i_r=i_{r+1}$ and $p_r(i):=(i_r-i_{r+1}+y_r-y_{r+1})^{-1}$ otherwise (degenerate case), resp. $P_r(i):=1$ if $i_r=i_{r+1}$ and $P_r(i):=(1-q)(1-y_r(i)y_{r+1}(i)^{-1})^{-1}$ with $y_r(i):=q^{i_r}(1-y_r)$ otherwise (nondegenerate case), satisfy (3.23)-(3.25) resp. (4.24)-(4.26), (4.28)-(4.30) and (4.32); and the intertwining elements $\varphi_r:=\sum_i(s_r+p_r(i))e(i)$, resp. $\Phi_r:=\sum_i(T_r+P_r(i))e(i)$, satisfy all identities (3.14)-(3.20) of [BK Lemma 3.1], resp. (4.14)-(4.20) of [BK Lemma 4.1]. (iii) There exist invertible power series $q_r(i)\in F[[y_r,y_{r+1}]]$ (resp. $Q_r(i)$) satisfying (3.27)-(3.29), resp. (4.33)-(4.35); the explicit candidates (3.30) resp. (4.36) do, and for them the identity (3.43) resp. (4.44) holds.
items.strategy: This is [BK Sections 3.2-3.3 and 4.2-4.3]. (i) On the component $e(i)$ the generator $X_r$ has generalised eigenvalue $q^{i_r}$ (resp. $x_r$ has $i_r$) by the spectral construction of [[def-cyclotomic-hecke-central-content-sector-notation]], so $(1-q^{-i_r}X_r)$ acts nilpotently on $e(i)$ and $y_r^N=\sum_i y_r^Ne(i)=0$ for $N\gg0$; the $y$'s commute because the polynomial generators do. (ii) The displayed definitions are the source's (3.22)/(4.27); the identities (3.23)-(3.25), (4.24)-(4.30) and (4.32) are proven by expanding in $F[[y_r,y_{r+1}]]$ and clearing denominators, exactly as the source does (all divisions are by units). The intertwiner identities (3.14)-(3.20)/(4.14)-(4.20) are Lemma 3.1/4.1 and are verified by the same case-by-case computations, using the divided-difference convention $\partial_r(f)=(s_rf-f)/(y_r-y_{r+1})$ of [BK (2.1)]. (iii) Verifying (3.27)-(3.29)/(4.33)-(4.35) for the displayed candidates (3.30)/(4.36) is a finite computation in $F[[y_r,y_{r+1}]]$ using (3.23)-(3.25)/(4.24)-(4.26) and (3.28)/(4.34); (3.43)/(4.44) is the source's displayed consequence of (1.14) and (3.28)/(4.34). No choice is used. Every quotient in the explicit source choices is a formal polynomial division whose numerator is divisible by its displayed dot difference; each resulting series has nonzero constant coefficient. On unequal colors the spectral-value denominators are units. On equal colors the fixed DG q_r is 1+y_(r+1)−y_r, and fixed NG Q_r is 1−q_H+q_H y_(r+1)−y_r (no extra denominator). Thus finite nilpotent evaluation is valid over F itself. Source compatibility is a polynomial/rational-unit identity, so no algebraic closure or square root is used.

items.title: The cyclotomic KLR block satisfies the affine Hecke relations
items.statement: In the specialized cyclotomic KLR content algebra $R^\Lambda_\alpha$ define $x_r:=\sum_{i\in I_\alpha}(y_r+i_r)e(i)$ and $s_r:=\sum_{i\in I_\alpha}(\psi_rq_r(i)-p_r(i))e(i)$ (degenerate case), resp. $X_r:=\sum_{i\in I_\alpha}q^{i_r}(1-y_r)e(i)$ and $T_r:=\sum_{i\in I_\alpha}(\psi_rQ_r(i)-P_r(i))e(i)$ (nondegenerate case), where $p,P,q,Q$ are the power series of [[lem-cyclotomic-hecke-intertwiners-and-local-power-series]] evaluated in $R^\Lambda_\alpha$ using the nilpotence of the $y$'s. Then these elements satisfy the defining relations (3.2)-(3.5), resp. (4.2)-(4.5), of the affine Hecke algebra and the cyclotomic relation $\prod_i(x_1-i)^{\lambda_i}=0$, resp. $\prod_i(X_1-q^i)^{\lambda_i}=0$; hence they define a unique $F$-algebra homomorphism $\sigma:H^\Lambda_d\to R^\Lambda_\alpha$. Moreover $\sigma$ kills $e_\beta$ and every corner component $e_\beta H^\Lambda_de_\gamma$ with $(\beta,\gamma)\ne(\alpha,\alpha)$, and restricts to a unital homomorphism $\sigma:H^\Lambda_\alpha\to R^\Lambda_\alpha$ with $\sigma(e(i))=e(i)$ for $i\in I_\alpha$ and $\sigma(e(i))=0$ otherwise.
items.strategy:
This is [BK Theorem 3.3 with Lemma 3.4] (degenerate) and [BK Theorem 4.3 with Section 4.5] (nondegenerate). (a) The mixed, quadratic and braid relations among the displayed elements are the source's explicit five-case expansions, using (1.12)-(1.14), (3.43)/(4.44) and the defining properties (3.27)-(3.29)/(4.33)-(4.35) of the normalising power series; the cyclotomic relation vanishes because $y_1^{(\Lambda,\alpha_{i_1})}e(i)=0$ is (1.6). (b) $R^\Lambda_\alpha$ is finite dimensional by [[lem-cyclotomic-klr-dot-annihilators-and-finite-root-strings]], so the homomorphism makes it a finite-dimensional $H^\Lambda_d$-module; the weight space of $\sigma(x_r)=y_r+(\text{colour})$ on it is exactly $e(i)R^\Lambda_\alpha$ when $i\in I_\alpha$ and $0$ otherwise (nilpotence of the $y$'s and (1.7)); hence $\sigma(e(i))$ is an idempotent projecting onto $e(i)R^\Lambda_\alpha$, so $\sigma(e(i))=e(i)$ for $i\in I_\alpha$ and $\sigma(e(i))=0$ otherwise. (c) Since $e_\alpha$ is central and $\sum_\beta e_\beta=1$ ([[def-cyclotomic-hecke-central-content-sector-notation]]), $\sigma(1-e_\alpha)=0$ and $\sigma$ annihilates all components with $(\beta,\gamma)\ne(\alpha,\alpha)$; it therefore factors through $H^\Lambda_\alpha$ and is unital there. No choice is used.

All-equal-color source exercise filled locally. 
The full BK source proof §§3–4 was read, including its explicitly omitted all-equal cases. They have this short local calculation. Write A=ψ_1, B=ψ_2, variables u,y_2=z,w, and ∂_a f=(s_a f−f)/(y_a−y_(a+1)). Already verified mixed/quadratic relations give fA=A s_1 f+∂_1 f, fB=B s_2 f+∂_2 f, A²=B²=0. Set

a=c−u+q_H z, b=c−z+q_H w, k=c−u+q_H w,

using (q_H,c)=(1,1) in DG and c=1−q_H in NG. On the all-equal component the Hecke generator is H_1=Aa−1,H_2=Bb−1. The relevant finite derivatives are

∂_2 a=−q_H, s_2a=k; ∂_1b=−1,s_1b=k;
∂_1k=1,s_1k=b; ∂_2k=q_H,s_2k=a;
∂_1a=∂_2b=q_H+1.

In particular ∂_1(kb)=0 and ∂_2(ka)=0. Expand the eight terms of each triple, move polynomials to the right with these identities, and remove A²,B². The exact two expressions are

H_1H_2H_1=ABA·abk−AB·kb−BA·ka+A(a+q_H b)+B(a+b)−1,
H_2H_1H_2=BAB·abk−AB·kb−BA·ka+A(a+q_H b)+B(a+b)−1.

Therefore H_1H_2H_1−H_2H_1H_2=(ABA−BAB)abk. The product abk is a UNIT in the actual nilpotent-variable algebra: its constant is1 in DG or(1−q_H)³≠0 in NG. In the forward direction Hecke braid implies the required ψ braid by multiplication by that inverse. In the inverse direction the established ψ braid implies Hecke braid. The same mixed rule gives H_i²=(q_H−1)H_i+q_H in NG and H_i²=1 in DG (the relation is uniform at q_H=1). Hence no unproved “Case5: exercise” remains at the actual consumer seam. The source's remaining four color-pattern cases have full explicit expansions in the retrieved §§3–4; their outer-equal unequal-middle correction is the polynomial in §1, not its negative.

items.title: Hecke intertwiners produce the local KLR generators
items.statement: Let $H^\Lambda_\alpha$ be a central content sector, possibly zero, as in [[def-cyclotomic-hecke-central-content-sector-notation]] and let $y_r$ be the elements of [[lem-cyclotomic-hecke-intertwiners-and-local-power-series]]. Put $\psi_r:=\sum_{i\in I_\alpha}\varphi_rq_r(i)^{-1}e(i)$ (degenerate case) resp. $\psi_r:=\sum_{i\in I_\alpha}\Phi_rQ_r(i)^{-1}e(i)$ (nondegenerate case). Then the elements $\{e(i):i\in I_\alpha\}\cup\{y_1,\dots,y_d\}\cup\{\psi_1,\dots,\psi_{d-1}\}$ of $H^\Lambda_\alpha$ satisfy the relations (1.6)-(1.15) of the sign-modified cyclotomic KLR presentation. Consequently there is a unique $F$-algebra homomorphism $\rho:R^\Lambda_\alpha\to H^\Lambda_\alpha$ with $e(i)\mapsto e(i)$, $y_r\mapsto y_r$ and $\psi_r\mapsto\psi_r$.

The relations listed are exactly the presentation of $R^\Lambda_\alpha$ established in [[def-type-a-cyclotomic-specialization-of-the-qg-klr-algebras]], so the universal property gives the unique $\rho$. No choice is used.

items.title: Central content sectors are isomorphic to cyclic type-A cyclotomic KLR algebras
items.statement: Over any field F in the charged finite-e conventions, the explicit maps ρ:R^Λ_α→H^Λ_α and σ:H^Λ_α→R^Λ_α from the preceding forward and inverse relation lemmas are mutually inverse, for every content α, including zero sectors. Here H^Λ_α is only the central CRT content sector; no primitivity is assumed. Thus H^Λ_α=0 iff R^Λ_α=0, and summing over finite height-d contents gives H^Λ_d≅⊕_α R^Λ_α. On idempotents the maps are literal identity, and the dot image is x_r−i_r (DG) or 1−q_H^(−i_r)X_r (NG). This result precedes the late dimension/basis and primitive-block theorems. No algebraic closure hypothesis is required.
items.strategy: The two declared relation lemmas construct the maps over F from finite nilpotent evaluations of explicit invertible-constant source series. The CRT spectrum splits over the actual c_i, not an algebraic closure. In R the inverse polynomial generators have exactly the eigenword projectors e(ν), because nilpotent dots shift those distinct scalar eigenvalues; their regular-module CRT projectors therefore are e(ν), with zero on other contents. Hence σ(e_α)=1_R and σ annihilates every other central sector. The restriction is unital. For generator composites, σρ(y_r)=y_r and ρσ(z_r)=z_r by the finite sum of projectors. On crossings, σ(Φ_r Q_r^(-1)e(ν))=(ψ_r Q_r−P_r+P_r)Q_r^(-1)e(ν)=ψ_r e(ν); the reverse composite sends ψ_r Q_r−P_r to Φ_r−P_r=T_r (or s_r), on each word. These are literal ordered expressions, not a commutation of ψ with its coefficient. Thus the composites fix all presentation generators and are identity. If H_α=0, the already constructed σ satisfies σ(e_α)=1_R, forcing1_R=0; conversely the forward inverse identities force H_α=0 if R_α=0. Zero rings and rankzero are therefore included without a nonzero-block premise. Neither exact dimension nor primitive terminology has entered this proof. The full source color-case verifications and the completed all-equal eight-term calculation reside in the declared preceding local relation lemmas.

items.title: The regular Hom norm gives the total cyclotomic KLR dimension in cyclic type A
items.statement: Let $F$ be any field, $I=\mathbb Z/e\mathbb Z$ with finite $e\ge2$, and use the standard homogeneous cyclotomic KLR quotient at $\Lambda=\sum_i\lambda_i\Lambda_i$ for the cyclic affine type-A Cartan datum and admissible graded parameters. Put $\ell=\sum_i\lambda_i$ and $B_d=\bigoplus_{\operatorname{ht}\beta=d}R^\Lambda(\beta)$. Then $\dim_F B_d=\ell^d d!$ for $d>0$, and $B_0=F$ has dimension one. The proof uses the basic first induction-restriction adjunction and mixed relations on projective $K_0$ modulo $v-1$, where $v$ is the formal grading variable, independent of any Hecke parameter $q_H$. No Frobenius theorem, tensor-form perfectness, highest-weight/global-basis isometry or Hecke basis is required. If $\ell=0,d>0$, then $B_d=0$.
items.strategy:
Proof. Work in projective K0 modulo v−1, so shifts are identified. Write P_d=[B_d], P_0=[F], D=Σ_i F_i^basic, E=Σ_i E_i^basic. All sums are finite. For A=R^Λ(β), B=R^Λ(β+i), and the right-append corner e=e(β,i), multiplication gives Be⊗_A A≅Be with inverse b↦b⊗1_A. This uses only the unital corner homomorphism A→eBe, not its injectivity. For fixed rank d, the e(β,i) over all β,i are orthogonal and sum to 1_{B_d}; each word has exactly one last color and prefix root. Thus ⊕_{β,i}B_de(β,i)=B_d and P_d=DP_{d−1}=D^dP_0. The zero-corner case gives Be=0 and is included.

The actual same-color categorical decomposition, forgetting its grading shifts, gives [E_i,F_i]=h_i(Λ−β)·Id on root component β for either sign of h_i. Its positive identity summands contribute h_i copies, its negative identity summands contribute the signed counterpart. The unequal-color mixed relation gives [E_i,F_j]=0 for i≠j after its shift is forgotten. Equivalently these are the integral v=1 mixed relations: [h_i]_v specializes to the integer h_i; there is no division by v−v^{-1}. For affine type A every Cartan column sums to zero, also for the double-edge e=2 matrix. Hence Σ_i h_i(Λ−β)=Σ_i λ_i−Σ_j β_jΣ_i a_{ij}=ℓ at every root component. Therefore [E,D]=ℓ·Id. Since rank-zero restriction is zero, EP_0=0. Expanding [E,D^d] gives EP_d=dℓ P_{d−1}.

For finite graded projectives define h(P,Q)=dim_F Hom(P,Q) with grading forgotten, equivalently evaluate the total graded Hom Hilbert series at v=1. Every ungraded map between these finite graded modules is the finite sum of its homogeneous parts. This integer-valued pairing is additive in both variables and unchanged by shifts, so descends to the stated K0 quotient. Pair distinct root blocks by zero and sum over each fixed rank. Ordinary tensor-Hom adjunction F_i^basic⊣E_i^basic gives h(F_iP,Q)=h(P,E_iQ), hence h(DP,Q)=h(P,EQ). All restricted modules remain finite projectives by the actual projectivity clauses, so the recurrence is inside the declared group. Now

h(P_d,P_d)=h(DP_{d−1},P_d)=h(P_{d−1},EP_d)=dℓ·h(P_{d−1},P_{d−1}).

The initial value is h(P_0,P_0)=dim_F End_F(F)=1. Finally End_{B_d}(B_d)≅B_d^op by right multiplication, so h(P_d,P_d)=dim_F B_d. Induction gives dim_F B_d=ℓ^d d! as an ordinary integer. Nothing reduces the integer dimension or dℓ inside F, so the argument includes every field characteristic. For ℓ=0,d>0 the recurrence gives B_d=0. For d=0, independently of ℓ, B_0=F and its basis is the singleton empty monomial; no 0^0 convention is required.

items.statement: With the conventions of [[def-affine-and-cyclotomic-type-a-hecke-algebras]], the images of the ordered monomials $x_1^{m_1}\cdots x_d^{m_d}w$ with $0\le m_r<\ell$, $w\in S_d$ (degenerate case) respectively $X_1^{m_1}\cdots X_d^{m_d}T_w$ with $0\le m_r<\ell$, $w\in S_d$ (nondegenerate case) form an $F$-basis of $H^\Lambda_d$. In particular $\dim_F H^\Lambda_d=\ell^d d!$ and $H^\Lambda_d$ is finite dimensional. For d=0 the singleton empty word gives H^Λ_0=F and dimension one independently of ℓ. E(unit)=0 and F^d(unit) is the regular rank-d algebra since last-color corner idempotents partition its identity (no corner injectivity assumed). Hence h(F^d unit,F^d unit)=dℓ h(F^(d−1)unit,F^(d−1)unit), starting at1; this is the integer ℓ^d d!, not an equality reduced modulo characteristic. Transfer this dimension through the early BK isomorphism. A spanning family of that cardinality in that-dimensional F-space is a basis. The late theorem does not feed CRT or early BK, and uses no Frobenius/global highest-weight isometry. Rank-zero and level-zero cases are checked directly as stated.
